questions.q: What mistake does the broken pull request's customers.sql introduce?
options: A syntax error that prevents the model from compiling at all
A typo in the customer_id column name
A missing source() declaration
A join fanout — joining orders directly to payments on order_id without aggregating payments first
questions.explain: The broken version joins payments directly instead of routing through the already-aggregated int_orders__payment_summary, producing a fanout.

questions.q: Why does a join fanout produce a plausible-looking wrong number instead of an obvious error?
options: Because Snowflake silently ignores all JOIN clauses
Because customer_id becomes NULL for every row
Because dbt automatically rounds all aggregated values
Because an order with multiple payment rows produces multiple joined rows, inflating counts and sums without throwing any error — the query runs successfully, just over duplicated rows
questions.explain: The SQL is syntactically valid and executes without error — the row duplication just silently inflates the aggregated totals.

questions.q: Which existing test actually catches this specific incident in CI?
options: unique on customers.customer_id, since the fanout produces more than one row per customer
non_negative on orders.amount
payment_method_is_valid
not_null on order_date
questions.explain: A customer with a multi-payment order now has duplicate rows in customers, which is exactly what the unique test on customer_id is designed to catch.

questions.q: What does the CI log actually show when this test fails?
options: A generic "build failed" message with no further detail
A message saying Power BI could not connect to Snowflake
The specific test name (unique_customers_customer_id) and the real count of rows that violated it, e.g. "Got 14 results, configured to fail if != 0"
Only a warning, since unique tests never block a build
questions.explain: dbt's test failure output names the specific test and the real violating row count — not a vague failure.

questions.q: What happens to this pull request as a direct result of Lesson 21's required status check?
options: Its Merge button stays disabled, so the broken model never reaches main, PROD, or Power BI
The incident only becomes visible after the change is already live in Power BI
It merges automatically after a short delay
GitHub automatically reverts the commit without notifying anyone
questions.explain: The required status check blocks the merge through GitHub's own UI — the whole point of Chapter 6's work, now proven against a real mistake.
